newsitem.title: MEXICO: Top Mexico banks see first flickers of loan demand.
newsitem.headline: Top Mexico banks see first flickers of loan demand.

text.p: After a long absence, the first flickers of loan demand showed up in the reports of Mexico's top two banks in the second quarter, but asset quality continued to blur the horizon, especially at Banamex.

Both Grupo Financiero Banamex Accival and Grupo Financiero Bancomer reported strong increases in profits in the second quarter, but the numbers were bolstered by one-time trading gains because of a rallying stock market.
The good news singled out by several analysts was a fledgling recovery in commercial loan demand that had been snuffed out in the aftermath of the December 1994 peso crisis.
That suggested banks may be on the verge of real growth, rather than just struggling to shake off the stigma of crisis.

"We're starting to see some growth. We're seeing a recovery in fees and we can view that as a leading indicator of growth in the economy," said Susana Ornelas, banking analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Mexico City.
"From looking at the figures, an increase in loan demand looks probable. There was a real increase in commercial loans at both banks and I view that as pretty encouraging."

In a report issued late Thursday, Bancomer -- the second largest of the two banks -- said its loan portfolio, excluding credits sold to the government, grew by 0.73 percent in the second quarter compared with the first quarter, the first increase in that area in more than two years.
It had a 3.3 percent increase in commercial loans, while commercial loans at Banamex grew 5 percent.

"We are shifting from banking system recovery into sustainable growth," said Brent Erensel, bank analyst at UBS Securities in New York. "Deposit and loan growth moves you into the next stage of the cycle."

He raised his earnings per share estimate on Banacci in 1997 to 2.50 pesos from 2 pesos and to 3.0 pesos in 1998 from 2.50, even though he acknowledged that net interest income will decline going forward due to a mortgage discount program.
Other analysts were less optimistic about the bank's earnings performance, and some were clearly concerned aabout its asset quality, especially compared with Bancomer.

During the second quarter, Banamex's past-due loans before charge-offs rose 16 percent, compared with a five percent increase at Bancomer. Banamex's delinquent mortgage past-dues rose a staggering 27 percent.

Reflecting the increased weight of mortgages among past-due loans, Banamex's reserve coverage ratio fell to 55 percent in the second quarter compared with 59 percent in Q1. At Bancomer, it held steady at 57.5 percent.

"The real story here is asset quality and it appears Bancomer has been able to maintain it at a considerably stronger level than Banamex," said Andrew Collins, bank analyst at Credit Lyonnais in Mexico City.
"Bancomer restructured (past-due loans) more aggresively and faster, and it's starting to show now."

To deal with the problem, Banamex has launched a mortgage program offering borrowers up to 25 percent discounts on their monthly home payments if they are current on their payments, while those who are in arrears and become current will receive a 20 percent discount.
Analysts said the program is more attractive to borrowers than Bancomer's, and should help turn around Banamex's past-due loan problems and cut loan provisioning in the future.

But it also will have a negative impact on the bank's interest income because of the discounts offered. This could make Bancomer even more attractive if that bank is not forced by its customers to launch a similar product, analysts said.
